guidelineTitle: Treatment of restless legs syndrome and periodic limb movement disorder: an AASM clinical practice guideline
recommendation: Good practice statement: test serum iron studies, including ferritin and transferrin saturation, in all patients with clinically significant RLS, ideally in the morning. Consensus thresholds for adults: oral or IV iron if ferritin ≤ 75 ng/mL or transferrin saturation < 20%; IV iron only if ferritin is 75-100 ng/mL. Children: supplement if ferritin < 50 ng/mL. 'These iron supplementation guidelines are different than for the general population.'

numbersToVerify: adult threshold ferritin ≤ 75 ng/mL or TSAT < 20% (oral or IV)

notes: The guideline says these thresholds are consensus-based and 'have not been empirically tested'. They are higher than the usual ferritin cut-offs for iron deficiency, so a 'normal' ferritin can still warrant iron in RLS.

body: US Food and Drug Administration (FDA): Xywav and Xyrem REMS
guidelineTitle: Xywav and Xyrem (oxybates) Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy
recommendation: Goal: to 'mitigate the risks of serious adverse outcomes resulting from inappropriate prescribing, misuse, abuse, and diversion.' Prescribers must enroll and submit a product-specific prescription form. Patients must enroll. Only certified pharmacies may dispense, they ship directly to the patient, and they check for duplicate oxybate prescriptions. First shipment is capped at 30 days, later ones at 90 days.

body: NHS England Specialised Commissioning (Clinical Reference Group for Paediatric Neurosciences)
guidelineTitle: Clinical Commissioning Policy: Sodium oxybate for symptom control of narcolepsy with cataplexy (children and adolescents aged 7 until 19 years)
recommendation: Funded only 'where attempts to control symptoms of narcolepsy with cataplexy have failed despite a trial of first and second line medications from each symptom group for at least three months'. Requires an ICSD-3 diagnosis, treated comorbid sleep disorders on polysomnogram, and MDT approval. Use is tracked (e.g. Blueteq). Stop if there is respiratory depression or an incomplete response at 3 months. After the 19th birthday, funding passes to local commissioners (CCGs/ICBs).

conflictsOfInterest: not stated
notes: Its claim of no advantage for extended-release melatonin sits against the EMA licensing a prolonged-release paediatric product (Slenyto). Bruni 2019 (PMID 31638842, narrative review) adds that 'no sleep medications [are] approved by the [FDA]' for pediatric insomnia and only one by the EMA.

guidelineTitle: Slenyto (prolonged-release melatonin) EPAR
recommendation: Indicated for 'insomnia in children and adolescents aged 2-18 years with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and / or neurogenetic disorders with aberrant diurnal melatonin secretion and /or nocturnal awakenings', and for 'insomnia in children and adolescents aged 6-17 years with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)', where sleep hygiene measures have been insufficient.

citation.authors: European Medicines Agency
citation.title: Slenyto: EPAR

conflictsOfInterest: not stated
numbersToVerify: when the ADHD indication was added (not stated on page)
notes: The original 2018 indication was ASD and/or Smith-Magenis syndrome (per the TGA AusPAR summary). The ADHD and neurogenetic wording appears to be a later extension; verify the date. The US has no approved paediatric hypnotic.

guidelineTitle: AusPAR: Slenyto (melatonin)
status: current; a 2026 AusPAR reportedly extends the indication
recommendation: The 2020 approval covers insomnia in ages 2-18 with ASD and/or Smith-Magenis syndrome, where sleep hygiene is insufficient. Starting dose is 2 mg, maximum 10 mg. Prescription only. A TGA decision of 15 May 2026 reportedly extends this to neurogenetic disorders and adds ADHD for ages 6-17.

citation.authors: TGA
citation.title: AusPAR: melatonin (Slenyto)

whatWasRead: secondary source (search-result summary; the TGA PDFs timed out)
conflictsOfInterest: not stated
notes: BLOCKED: open https://www.tga.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-07/auspar-slenyto-260713.pdf in Chrome. Do not ship the 2026 extension claim until it has been read.

body: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare / PMDA (Nobelpharma product Melatobel)
guidelineTitle: Melatobel (melatonin granules) approval
recommendation: Melatonin granules (Melatobel) are approved in Japan for sleep-onset difficulty in children with neurodevelopmental disorders. The pivotal study was a 26-week, uncontrolled, open-label phase III trial in 99 children aged 6-15, using 1, 2 or 4 mg. Sleep-onset latency shortened by a mean of 36.7 minutes.

citation.authors: Yuge K, Nagamitsu S, Ishikawa Y, et al.
citation.title: Long-term melatonin treatment for the sleep problems and aberrant behaviors of children with neurodevelopmental disorders

whatWasRead: abstract (trial); approval facts from secondary source (search results); PMDA label not read
conflictsOfInterest: Trial funded by and co-authored with Nobelpharma employees.
numbersToVerify: indicated age range on the label
notes: Melatonin is not sold as a supplement in Japan. The only approved product is this paediatric neurodevelopmental one.

body: Danish Health Authority (Sundhedsstyrelsen) national clinical guideline panel
guidelineTitle: Use of melatonin in children and adolescents with idiopathic chronic insomnia: systematic review, meta-analysis and clinical recommendation
recommendation: For otherwise healthy children aged 5-20: 'Melatonin should never be the first choice of treatment for this particular population, yet carefully monitored short-term use may be considered if sleep hygiene practices and non-pharmacological interventions have proven inadequate, and only if daytime function is compromised.'

citation.authors: Edemann-Callesen H, Andersen HK, Ussing A, et al.
citation.title: Use of melatonin in children and adolescents with idiopathic chronic insomnia: a systematic review, meta-analysis, and clinical recommendation

conflictsOfInterest: Funded by the Danish Health Authority and the Parker Institute (Oak Foundation). One panelist sits on the Danish medication reimbursement committee, and one had honoraria from AGB Pharma, Takeda and Medice.
notes: The most restrictive national position found, set off by rising melatonin prescriptions for children. Compare the AASM 2015 weak-for recommendation for DSWPD in children, and US over-the-counter use. The direction is coded 'suggest against' as first-line; check against the Danish source.

body: Danish Health Authority (Sundhedsstyrelsen) national clinical guideline panel
guidelineTitle: Use of melatonin for children and adolescents with chronic insomnia attributable to disorders beyond indication
recommendation: For ages 2-20 with insomnia from other (mainly medical) disorders, excluding ASD/ADHD-only populations: off-label melatonin 'should never be the first choice of treatment, but may be considered by medical specialists with knowledge of the underlying disorder and if non-pharmacological interventions are inadequate.' Follow-up is essential.

citation.authors: Edemann-Callesen H, Andersen HK, Ussing A, et al.
citation.title: Use of melatonin for children and adolescents with chronic insomnia attributable to disorders beyond indication: a systematic review, meta-analysis and clinical recommendation

conflictsOfInterest: Funded by the Danish Health Authority and the Parker Institute (Oak Foundation). One panelist sits on the Danish medication reimbursement committee, and one had honoraria from AGB Pharma, Takeda and Medice.
notes: Coded as a pathway row because it says who should start the drug: specialists, not GPs.

guidelineTitle: Guidelines on physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep for children under 5 years of age
recommendation: Infants: '14–17h (0–3 months of age) or 12–16h (4–11 months of age) of good quality sleep, including naps.' Ages 1-2: '11-14 hours of good quality sleep, including naps, with regular sleep and wake-up times.' Ages 3-4: '10–13h of good quality sleep, which may include a nap, with regular sleep and wake-up times.'

citation.authors: WHO
citation.title: Guidelines on physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep for children under 5 years of age

whatWasRead: summary page (WHO news release 24 Apr 2019; the full PDF on iris.who.int returned 403)
conflictsOfInterest: not stated
notes: Sleep-duration norm, not a treatment. Useful as the global baseline for 'how much sleep'.

guidelineTitle: Diagnosis and management of childhood obstructive sleep apnea syndrome
recommendation: 'All children/adolescents should be screened for snoring.' Polysomnography for snoring plus symptoms or signs. 'Adenotonsillectomy is recommended as the first-line treatment of patients with adenotonsillar hypertrophy.' CPAP if adenotonsillectomy is not done or OSA persists. Weight loss if overweight. 'Intranasal corticosteroids are an option' for mild OSA when surgery is contraindicated, or for mild post-operative OSA.

citation.authors: Marcus CL, Brooks LJ, Draper KA, et al.; American Academy of Pediatrics
citation.title: Diagnosis and management of childhood obstructive sleep apnea syndrome

conflictsOfInterest: not stated
notes: Written for primary care. China 2020 gives montelukast and nasal steroids a much bigger role, and France 2023 does not require a sleep study.

body: American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery Foundation (AAO-HNSF)
guidelineTitle: Clinical Practice Guideline: Tonsillectomy in Children (Update)
recommendation: Refer for polysomnography before tonsillectomy if the child is '<2 years of age' or has 'obesity, Down syndrome, craniofacial abnormalities, neuromuscular disorders, sickle cell disease, or mucopolysaccharidoses'. 'Clinicians should recommend tonsillectomy for children with obstructive sleep apnea documented by overnight polysomnography.' Overnight inpatient monitoring if '<3 years old or have severe obstructive sleep apnea (apnea-hypopnea index ≥10 obstructive events/hour, oxygen saturation nadir <80%, or both)'.

citation.authors: Mitchell RB, Archer SM, Ishman SL, et al.
citation.title: Clinical Practice Guideline: Tonsillectomy in Children (Update)

conflictsOfInterest: not stated
numbersToVerify: inpatient monitoring if < 3 years or AHI ≥ 10 or nadir < 80%
notes: It also says codeine must not be given to children under 12 after tonsillectomy. Unlike the AAP, it does not require a sleep study for every otherwise healthy child.

guidelineTitle: Obstructive sleep disordered breathing in 2- to 18-year-old children: diagnosis and management
recommendation: Severity measured objectively, 'preferably using polysomnography'. Children with 'AHI >5 episodes·h-1, those with an AHI of 1-5 episodes·h-1 and the presence of morbidity or factors predicting SDB persistence, and children with complex conditions (e.g. Down syndrome and Prader-Willi syndrome) all appear to benefit from treatment'. Treatment is 'stepwise' with re-evaluation after each step.

citation.authors: Kaditis AG, Alonso Alvarez ML, Boudewyns A, et al.
citation.title: Obstructive sleep disordered breathing in 2- to 18-year-old children: diagnosis and management

conflictsOfInterest: not stated
notes: Compared with the AAP, this frames treatment by morbidity and risk rather than 'adenotonsillectomy first'.

guidelineTitle: ERS statement on obstructive sleep disordered breathing in 1- to 23-month-old children
status: stale (2017); a 2024 Eur Respir Rev update exists (PMID 38296343, not read)
recommendation: Severity measured 'preferably by polysomnography, or alternatively polygraphy or nocturnal oximetry'. 'Adenotonsillectomy and continuous positive airway pressure are the most frequently used treatment measures', along with targeted interventions such as 'supraglottoplasty for laryngomalacia or nasopharyngeal airway for mandibular hypoplasia'.

citation.authors: Kaditis AG, Alonso Alvarez ML, Boudewyns A, et al.
citation.title: ERS statement on obstructive sleep disordered breathing in 1- to 23-month-old children

conflictsOfInterest: None declared.
notes: The only formal guidance found for infants under 2.

guidelineTitle: Management of Persistent, Post-adenotonsillectomy Obstructive Sleep Apnea in Children: An Official ATS Clinical Practice Guideline
recommendation: 'up to 40% of children may have persistent OSA' after adenotonsillectomy. Six conditional suggestions: CPAP if not suited to site-specific surgery; orthodontic or dentofacial treatment for specific craniofacial features; weight loss if obese; lingual tonsillectomy; supraglottoplasty for sleep-dependent laryngomalacia; 'children on intranasal steroids with persistent OSA may be treated with montelukast'.
strength: Conditional, very low certainty (all six; GRADE)

citation.authors: Ehsan Z, Ishman SL, Soghier I, et al.
citation.title: Management of Persistent, Post-adenotonsillectomy Obstructive Sleep Apnea in Children: An Official American Thoracic Society Clinical Practice Guideline
citation.journal: Am J Respir Crit Care Med

conflictsOfInterest: Funded by ATS. Almeida is on the Somnomed clinical advisory board; no other conflicts.
notes: The panel includes European members (Kaditis, Verhulst, Boudewyns). Montelukast carries an FDA boxed warning for neuropsychiatric events (2020; verify), which may explain its cautious place here compared with China.

body: Canadian Thoracic Society (CTS) / Canadian Sleep Society (CSS)
guidelineTitle: The CTS/CSS Guideline on the Diagnosis of Obstructive Sleep Apnea in Children
recommendation: 'The panel upholds polysomnography as the recommended standard'. 'Level 3/Home Sleep Apnea Testing is recommended as an alternative option to diagnose OSA in otherwise healthy children over 5-years of age for whom access to polysomnography is effectively absent.' The Pediatric Sleep Questionnaire and overnight oximetry 'should not be used to diagnose OSA in children'.

citation.authors: MacLean JE, Adeleye A, Van Dam A, et al.
citation.title: The Canadian Thoracic Society/Canadian Sleep Society Guideline on the Diagnosis of Obstructive Sleep Apnea in Children

conflictsOfInterest: Declared per CTS COI policy; details in supplement (not read).
notes: Driven by poor PSG access ('limited in many jurisdictions'). This is the first national guideline found to accept home testing for children.

body: French Society of Sleep Research and Medicine (SFRMS) expert group
guidelineTitle: Management of obstructive sleep apnea syndrome type 1 in children and adolescents - A French consensus
recommendation: 'A specialist otolaryngologist examination, including nasofibroscopy, is essential during diagnosis. A sleep study for OSA1 is not mandatory when at least two nighttime symptoms (including snoring) are noted.' ENT surgery is often required, and orthodontic treatment with orofacial myofunctional therapy may be indicated. Follow-up is multidisciplinary.

citation.authors: Aubertin G, Akkari M, Andrieux A, et al.
citation.title: Management of obstructive sleep apnea syndrome type 1 in children and adolescents - A French consensus

conflictsOfInterest: Several authors report speaker or travel fees or consultancies with CPAP and home-ventilation companies (ResMed, Elivie, Sefam, Philips Respironics, Nomics and others).
notes: CONTRAST: China 2020 says OSA 'cannot be diagnosed without' PSG. France lets symptoms plus an ENT exam stand in for a sleep study, and the US (AAP) sits in between.

body: Chinese Medical Association (ENT, Pediatrics, Pediatric Surgery societies)
guidelineTitle: Chinese guideline for the diagnosis and treatment of childhood obstructive sleep apnea (2020)
status: current (2020 version, published 2021; nearly 5 years old)
recommendation: 'pediatric OSA cannot be diagnosed without the use of polysomnography (PSG)' (1B). 'Obstructive apnea hypopnea index (OAHI) > 1/h is recommended as the threshold value' (1A). Severity: mild 1-5, moderate 5-10, severe >10 per hour (2B). Where PSG access is limited, portable monitoring such as a pulse oximeter is acceptable (2C). Questionnaires alone are not recommended.

citation.authors: Working Group of Chinese Guideline for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Childhood OSA (Chinese Medical Association)
citation.title: Chinese guideline for the diagnosis and treatment of childhood obstructive sleep apnea (2020)

conflictsOfInterest: All participants declare no financial or non-financial conflicts.
notes: Stricter than France 2023 on testing, but like Canada it allows portable tests where PSG is scarce.

body: Chinese Medical Association (ENT, Pediatrics, Pediatric Surgery societies)
guidelineTitle: Chinese guideline for the diagnosis and treatment of childhood obstructive sleep apnea (2020)
status: current (2020 version, published 2021; nearly 5 years old)
recommendation: Adenotonsillectomy is recommended for moderate or severe OSA with adenotonsillar hypertrophy (1B). For mild to moderate OSA, 'nasal corticosteroids or oral montelukast sodium are recommended to reduce sleep apnea events' (1B), and the two combined (2D), with regular follow-up.

citation.authors: Working Group of Chinese Guideline for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Childhood OSA (Chinese Medical Association)
citation.title: Chinese guideline for the diagnosis and treatment of childhood obstructive sleep apnea (2020)

conflictsOfInterest: All participants declare no financial or non-financial conflicts.
notes: KEY CONTRAST: China gives montelukast a 1B recommendation for mild to moderate OSA. The AAP 2012 lists only nasal steroids as an 'option', and ATS 2024 gives montelukast only a conditional, very-low-certainty suggestion for persistent OSA.
